findings.text: The opening paragraph tells a newcomer in plain words what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. Within a few lines they can say what Athena is and why it matters.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete and in order: what you need first, clone, install, try it. A link near the top jumps straight there, so the next step is easy to find.
findings.source: Next steps: "Get the code: git clone https://github.com/doodla/athena.git" / "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh" / "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page doesn't say whether `athena` is on the PATH after `./setup.sh`, which directory to run it from, or whether pressing Enter commits to the repository straight away. A cautious newcomer may hold off before running it on a real repo.
findings.source: Next steps: "press Enter to run it on your repository."

findings.text: The page says Athena records the models, cost and verdict for each step, but this study, which is the page's showcase, shows none of them. The newcomer sees the claim tracing but never an example of the accountability record the opening paragraph promises.
findings.source: "It is for people who want ... a commit they can trace to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict." vs footer "45 claims at commit 6407052f..."

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed state-machine study of firstmate, a different project, with exit codes, guards and places-held counters. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena may lose interest or wonder whether they are on the wrong page, even though the header explains that the study is a demonstration.
findings.source: Header: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project..." followed by sections States, Counters, Transitions t1–t12, Why it is built this way

findings.text: This header link talks to the site owner, not a visitor. A newcomer can't tell whether it applies to them.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: This section uses internal repository terms (study id, the `studies/` folder) that mean nothing to a first-time visitor.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."

findings.text: The page states openly what the study did not check and that nothing was run. That builds trust in the tracing claim, but a newcomer may not know what "marked read" means without looking up the glossary entry for mark.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths..." and f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: The wording here is awkward and makes a reader hunt for the explanation. The glossary and the "Words used first" list do define terms well, including honest gaps such as "this page gives no test for it" for in scope.
findings.source: Transitions lead-in: "The two deciders are explained below the cards' heading."
